answer:
ANALYSIS COMPLETE — HYPOTHESIS AND SUPPORTING RESULTS

HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, phrased for right-censored 1979 attainment)
In this NLSY79 extract, education is measured only as of 1979 (respondents then aged 14–22), so all "BA completion rates" below are attainment-as-of-1979, not life-course BA rates. Under the approved proxy (highest grade completed ≥16), BA completion is extremely rare (32 of 8,870 in the primary sample, 0.36%) and the data show no detectable Black advantage at any family-SES level: observed as-of-1979 BA rates for Black vs non-Black/non-Hispanic respondents are 0.10% vs 0.12% (Low SES), 0.65% vs 0.25% (Mid), and 0.29% vs 0.63% (High) — small, non-monotonic gaps (−0.02, +0.40, −0.34 pp) whose race×SES-tertile interactions are statistically indistinguishable (Firth logit interaction p = 0.42 and 0.71; MI-pooled p = 0.40 and 0.74). Family SES itself is a strong, race-similar escalator: the High-vs-Low SES log-odds of BA is +1.66 (p=0.026) and of any postsecondary exposure is +1.03 (p<0.001), with no significant race modification at any tertile. The only race-related advantage that the data support appears in the better-powered secondary outcome (any postsecondary exposure, grade ≥13): conditional on age and ASVAB achievement, Black respondents show HIGHER postsecondary exposure than non-Black/non-Hispanic respondents (race coefficient +1.08 log-odds, p<0.001), and this adjusted Black advantage is largest at Low/Mid SES and significantly attenuated at High SES (interaction −0.76, p=0.014). Unadjusted, however, Black postsecondary exposure is lower at every SES level, with the deficit widest at the top tertile (−6.4 pp at High vs −2.1 pp at Low) — a descriptive pattern whose interaction is not significant. Bottom line: the hypothesis this data can support is that attainment rises steeply with family-of-origin SES at a similar rate for Black and non-Black students, with no evidence that the (null-to-negative as-of-1979) Black–non-Black BA gap depends on SES level; any "Black advantage" is visible only after conditioning on age and achievement, and is concentrated at lower-to-middle SES.

KEY EVIDENCE
1. Observed rates by race × SES tertile (Wilson CIs in outputs/rate_table_*.csv):
- BA (≥16): Black 0.10 [0.02–0.56] / 0.65 [0.22–1.90] / 0.29 [0.05–1.62]; nonB-nonH 0.12 [0.03–0.44] / 0.25 [0.12–0.55] / 0.63 [0.40–0.98]; Hispanic 0.08 / 0.20 / 0.19 (descriptive only). Events: 1/3/1 Black; 2/6/19 nonB-nonH.
- Any postsecondary (≥13): Black 5.66 / 10.87 / 12.75; nonB-nonH 7.78 / 11.52 / 19.13; gaps −2.12 [se 0.98] / −0.65 [1.59] / −6.38 [1.93] pp.
- Grade ≥17: 2 events total — model non-estimable (descriptive only).
2. Firth logit (primary sample N=8,870: 1,812 Black, 7,058 nonB-nonH): BA — race_black −0.19 (p=0.87), ses_high +1.66 (p=0.026), race×ses_mid +1.15 (p=0.42), race×ses_high −0.59 (p=0.71). PS (≥13) — race_black −0.34 (p=0.038), ses_mid +0.43, ses_high +1.03 (both p≤0.001), interactions +0.28 (p=0.23) / −0.14 (p=0.55).
3. Covariate check (age_z + asvab_z, N=7,720): PS — race_black +1.08 (p<0.001), race×ses_high −0.76 (p=0.014); BA — interaction non-estimable (complete separation: no Black High-SES BA events in this subset); age_z +2.86 and asvab_z +1.46 (both p<0.001) confirm the sparsity problem.
4. Sensitivity: complete-case SES (N=5,553) and PMM multiple imputation (m=5, Rubin pooling) reproduce the same pattern (BA interactions p=0.43/0.91 complete-case, p=0.40/0.74 MI; PS main race effect −0.37/−0.41, interactions ns). Later-SES sensitivity (1985/89 income, 1985/90/96 wealth, winsorized at 1st/99th pct, never in the primary index): BA rates near zero everywhere (0–1.2%), with nominally higher Black High-SES cells (e.g., wealth 1996: Black High 1.21% vs nonB High 0.80%) but unstable, non-significant cell counts.
5. SES components by race (context: Black respondents sit lower in the SES distribution): parental education 9.03 vs 12.57 grades, log income 9.13 vs 9.34, occupation rank 4.80 vs 6.26 (Black vs nonB-nonH).

WORKFLOW (executed in analysis.py; outputs in outputs/)
Clean (95→missing) → define ba/ps/ba17 → composite SES (z-scored parental education = max of parents; log 1979 income top-coded at 75,001; occupation-at-14 mapped to 1-digit 1970 census major groups ranked 0 professional >2 managers >3 sales >4 clerical >5 craftsmen >6 operatives >1 farm managers >7 transport/laborers >9 service >8 farm laborers; mean of ≥2 of 3 available components; tertiles) → race × tertile rate tables with Wilson CIs → Firth-penalized logit with race×tertile interaction (manual implementation, intercept unpenalized) → age+ASVAB covariate check → complete-case and PMM-MI sensitivity → later-SES winsorized sensitivity → tertile gap tables.

LIMITATIONS (stated plainly)
- Education is right-censored at 1979: these are attainment-as-of-1979 rates (0.36% BA), not life-course BA rates; the BA question is severely under-powered (32 events; the ≥17 outcome has 2 events and is non-estimable).
- The Sample-ID × cohort cross-tab conflicts with the documented NLSY79 sampling design (military IDs 17–20 split across cohorts; Hispanic n=3,174 exceeds Black n=2,002, unlike the real oversample design); per instruction the file's coding is taken at face value and this is flagged as a provenance limitation.
- No occupation lookup table was supplied; a coarse 1-digit major-group ordinal ranking was used.
- Differential missingness by race (father's education 18–26% vs 8%; occupation 22–48%) handled via available-component averaging, complete-case, and PMM-MI; MAR assumed.
- Incomes top-coded (75,001 in 1979; 100,001 in 1985); wealth extremes winsorized only in sensitivity runs.
- The adjusted "Black advantage" in postsecondary exposure relies on ASVAB as an achievement control (a potential mediator), so its causal reading is limited.

Deliverables: analysis.py (executed, nonempty) plus 16 supporting CSV tables in outputs/ (rate tables, Firth models primary/covariate/complete-case/MI-pooled, tertile gap tables, later-SES sensitivity, SES-components-by-race).

payload.hypothesis: With education right-censored at 1979, as-of-1979 BA completion (highest grade >=16) is too rare (32/8,870) to show any Black advantage at any SES level: Black vs non-Black/non-Hispanic rates are 0.10% vs 0.12% (Low SES), 0.65% vs 0.25% (Mid), 0.29% vs 0.63% (High), and race x SES-tertile interactions are non-significant (p = 0.42/0.71; MI-pooled p = 0.40/0.74). Family-of-origin SES strongly raises attainment at a similar rate for both groups (High-vs-Low log-odds +1.66 for BA, +1.03 for any postsecondary, both significant). The only supported Black advantage appears in the secondary outcome (any postsecondary, >=13): conditional on age and ASVAB achievement, Black respondents show higher postsecondary exposure (+1.08 log-odds, p<0.001), an advantage largest at Low/Mid SES and significantly attenuated at High SES (interaction -0.76, p=0.014); unadjusted, Black postsecondary exposure is lower at every SES level with the widest deficit at High SES (-6.4 pp). Hypothesis: the Black-non-Black difference in college attainment in these data does not depend on SES level — SES is a common, race-similar escalator — and any Black advantage is detectable only after adjustment for age and achievement, concentrated at lower-to-middle SES.
payload.workflow: Clean (grade 95 -> missing) -> outcomes BA>=16, any postsecondary >=13, >=17 -> composite family-of-origin SES index (z-scored parental education max of parents, log 1979 family income top-coded 75,001, occupation-at-14 mapped to ranked 1-digit 1970 census major groups; mean of >=2 of 3 available; tertiles) -> race x tertile rate tables with Wilson CIs -> Firth-penalized logit with race x tertile interaction (intercept unpenalized) -> age+ASVAB covariate check -> complete-case and PMM multiple-imputation (m=5, Rubin pooling) sensitivity -> winsorized later-SES (1985/89 income, 1985/90/96 wealth) sensitivity -> tertile gap tables. All rates are attainment-as-of-1979, right-censored.
